newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: U.S., Singapore reach "open skies" agreement.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Singapore reach "open skies" agreement.

text.p: Officials from the United States and Singapore have initialled an "open skies" aviation agreement, the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore (CAAS) said on Thursday.
It said that under the deal, airlines of both countries could fly whichever routes they choose between Singapore and any point in the United States without restrictions on frequency.
The CAAS announcement followed two days of talks in Washington between officials of the two countries. The agreement is part of a wider U.S. effort to end curbs on air services throughout Asia.

"Singapore is pleased to be the first in Asia to conclude such an agreement with the U.S.," the CAAS quoted Communications Ministry Permanent Secretary Teo Ming Kian, who led the Singapore delegation, as saying.
The statement did not indicate when the agreement would go into effect. It said the U.S. delegation was expected to sign the deal soon at a ceremony in Singapore.
Singapore Airlines currently operates 39 weekly services between Singapore and the United States. Seven U.S. airlines operate a total of 49 weekly services between the two countries.
The CAAS said the seven U.S. carriers are United Airlines, Northwest Airlines, United Parcel Service, American International Airlines, Polar Air Cargo, Federal Express and Air Micronesia.
An "open skies" agreement would also allow additional carriers to start competing services.

Earlier in Washington, a U.S. Transportation Department official said the talks with Singapore followed an informal meeting last October in the city state, which included South Korea, Taiwan, Malaysia and Brunei.
The United States held exploratory talks with Japan, its major Asian aviation partner, on January 10-11, and is to hold further talks at an unspecified future date.
Liberalised U.S. aviation agreements, although not open skies accords, are already in effect with India and Thailand.

U.S. attention turned to Asia last year after a series of open skies agreements were reached with Canada, Germany and a number of smaller European countries. Talks are also being held with Britain, but so far with little apparent progress.
The U.S. aim to end curbs on flights to Asia, to the benefit of American carriers, is based on estimates that in the next 10 years traffic to Asia will exceed that to Europe.
The United States has argued that the world is turning towards ending restrictions on aviation services and that countries that resist this trend risk being left behind.
